questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes GLUE from MMLU in terms of what they evaluate in language models?
questions.choice_A: GLUE focuses on general NLU tasks like entailment and sentiment, whereas MMLU emphasizes multi-choice knowledge and reasoning across many academic subjects.
questions.choice_B: GLUE primarily measures few-shot instruction following, whereas MMLU focuses on dialogue safety and helpfulness.
questions.choice_C: GLUE evaluates multilingual translation quality, whereas MMLU evaluates code generation.
questions.choice_D: GLUE measures long-context retrieval, whereas MMLU measures tool-use reliability.

questions.question: What is a defining characteristic of Super-NaturalInstructions (S-NI) as an evaluation resource?
questions.choice_A: It is a single-task benchmark for question answering across scientific articles.
questions.choice_B: It aggregates thousands of crowdsourced tasks with natural language instructions that stress generalization across diverse instruction formats.
questions.choice_C: It is limited to code synthesis tasks with strict unit-test evaluation.
questions.choice_D: It focuses exclusively on multilingual translation pairs with BLEU scoring.

questions.question: How do Vicuna prompts and OASST1 (OpenAssistant) primarily differ as evaluation datasets?
questions.choice_A: Vicuna prompts target factual QA only, while OASST1 targets code generation.
questions.choice_B: Vicuna prompts are adversarial jailbreak tests, while OASST1 is a math benchmark.
questions.choice_C: Vicuna prompts are curated conversational prompts for subjective quality assessment, whereas OASST1 contains community-collected multi-turn assistant interactions with broader coverage and safety annotations.
questions.choice_D: Vicuna prompts are multilingual dialogues, whereas OASST1 is monolingual English-only chit-chat.

questions.question: Which is a key advantage of pairwise human preference comparisons over absolute rating scales (e.g., 1–5 Likert) when evaluating chatbot responses?
questions.choice_A: They require fewer annotations to estimate absolute quality levels.
questions.choice_B: They are immune to rater bias and cultural effects.
questions.choice_C: They directly produce calibrated, absolute scores comparable across datasets.
questions.choice_D: They reduce scale-use variance by asking raters to choose a better response, enabling more reliable relative rankings.

questions.question: When interpreting Fleiss' kappa for inter-annotator agreement, which statement is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Kappa adjusts observed agreement for chance, so a value near 0 indicates agreement close to chance-level even if raw agreement appears high due to class imbalance.
questions.choice_B: Kappa is simply the percentage of exact matches among raters.
questions.choice_C: Kappa is unaffected by the number of categories in the labeling scheme.
questions.choice_D: Kappa should always be above 0.8 for any valid annotation task.

questions.question: Which factor can artifactually depress Fleiss' kappa even when raters are reasonably consistent?
questions.choice_A: Having many raters per item.
questions.choice_B: Highly skewed label prevalence leading to high chance agreement.
questions.choice_C: Using clear, detailed annotation guidelines and training.
questions.choice_D: Aggregating labels with majority vote.

questions.question: What is a well-documented risk when using stronger LMs as judges to evaluate other models’ outputs?
questions.choice_A: They exhibit random scoring equivalent to coin flips.
questions.choice_B: They systematically underestimate longer responses compared to shorter ones.
questions.choice_C: They can show position and verbosity biases, and may favor models similar to themselves due to style alignment.
questions.choice_D: They cannot follow rubrics or chain-of-thought instructions.

questions.question: Which is a primary advantage and a primary limitation, respectively, of model-based evaluation using LMs as judges?
questions.choice_A: Advantage: perfect correlation with human judgments; Limitation: high monetary cost.
questions.choice_B: Advantage: guarantees absence of bias; Limitation: requires domain experts.
questions.choice_C: Advantage: direct access to ground truth; Limitation: infeasible for large datasets.
questions.choice_D: Advantage: scalable, fast, and cheap relative to human annotation; Limitation: can be prompt-sensitive and may encode biases not aligned with human preferences.

questions.question: In tournament-style pairwise evaluation of chatbots with Elo ratings, which assumption is most aligned with the Elo framework as commonly used?
questions.choice_A: The log-odds of model A beating model B is the difference in their latent skill parameters, implying a logistic win probability.
questions.choice_B: All pairwise matches are independent and identically distributed with Gaussian outcomes.
questions.choice_C: Elo requires a balanced round-robin schedule with equal matches between all pairs.
questions.choice_D: Elo cannot be updated online and needs a full batch of games to compute ratings.

questions.question: Which statistical model underlies many methods for aggregating pairwise preferences into a global ranking of models?
questions.choice_A: Poisson regression
questions.choice_B: Bradley–Terry model
questions.choice_C: Hidden Markov model
questions.choice_D: Gaussian mixture model

questions.question: When reporting uncertainty for accuracy on a multiple-choice benchmark with N items, which approach is generally appropriate?
questions.choice_A: Assume zero variance because accuracy is deterministic given predictions.
questions.choice_B: Use a t-test over per-item binary indicators regardless of N.
questions.choice_C: Compute a binomial proportion confidence interval (e.g., Wilson) for accuracy; for complex metrics, use nonparametric bootstrapping.
questions.choice_D: Report only the mean accuracy without variability to avoid clutter.

questions.question: Which bootstrapping practice helps produce more reliable confidence intervals for heterogeneous evaluation sets (e.g., multiple domains)?
questions.choice_A: Use the naive percentile bootstrap with a single global pool even when domains differ greatly.
questions.choice_B: Always resample at the token level rather than at the item level.
questions.choice_C: Apply parametric resampling from a normal approximation regardless of metric shape.
questions.choice_D: Use stratified or block bootstrapping to preserve domain composition and dependence structure when resampling.

questions.question: Why is it important to report multiple random seeds or prompt variations when evaluating instruction-following models?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the number of required test items.
questions.choice_B: It ensures models never overfit.
questions.choice_C: It captures variability due to stochastic decoding, prompt sensitivity, and few-shot exemplar selection, providing a more stable performance estimate.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees statistically significant improvements.

questions.question: When comparing many models across multiple benchmarks, which statistical consideration is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: Ignore dependence and treat all comparisons as independent to maximize power.
questions.choice_B: Control for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg) to limit family-wise error or false discovery rate.
questions.choice_C: Use only p-values below 0.10 to be conservative.
questions.choice_D: Report only the best-performing model to avoid selection bias.

questions.question: Which description of MMLU is most accurate for evaluation purposes?
questions.choice_A: A multi-subject, multi-choice benchmark spanning humanities, STEM, and professional domains that tests factual knowledge and reasoning under zero/few-shot settings.
questions.choice_B: A benchmark of long-context retrieval with citation requirements.
questions.choice_C: A conversational safety dataset focused on harmful content detection only.
questions.choice_D: A code-generation benchmark with unit-test based scoring.

questions.question: In assessing instruction-following quality for chatbots, which composite objective is often considered?
questions.choice_A: Throughput, latency, and GPU memory.
questions.choice_B: N-gram overlap, BLEU, and ROUGE only.
questions.choice_C: Helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness (sometimes summarized as "HHH") via human or model-judge preferences.
questions.choice_D: Perplexity on next-token prediction.

questions.question: Which scenario most clearly threatens the validity of benchmark evaluations due to data contamination?
questions.choice_A: Using a held-out test set drawn from the same distribution as training data.
questions.choice_B: Pretraining includes near-duplicates or exact copies of test questions and answers, inflating apparent generalization.
questions.choice_C: Using few-shot prompts from a related domain.
questions.choice_D: Evaluating with temperature 0 to reduce randomness.

questions.question: What is a best practice when instructing LMs-as-judges to mitigate known biases?
questions.choice_A: Avoid providing any rubric to prevent anchoring.
questions.choice_B: Use carefully designed rubrics with explicit criteria, randomized position of candidates, and chain-of-thought or justification prompts that are hidden from the scored models.
questions.choice_C: Always favor the longer response because it is likely more informative.
questions.choice_D: Use the same seed for all evaluations to ensure reproducibility at the expense of bias.

questions.question: When aggregating pairwise chatbot comparisons into a leaderboard, which statement is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Elo, TrueSkill, and Bradley–Terry all model latent skills but differ in handling uncertainty, priors, and draws.
questions.choice_B: Simple win-rate is always superior to model-based ratings.
questions.choice_C: Transitivity is guaranteed in empirical preferences, so cycles cannot occur.
questions.choice_D: Ratings are invariant to the match schedule.

questions.question: For a head-to-head A/B evaluation where raters choose the better answer, which significance test is most appropriate for testing whether A beats B more often than chance?
questions.choice_A: ANOVA on token probabilities.
questions.choice_B: Chi-square goodness-of-fit on continuous scores.
questions.choice_C: Binomial or exact sign test on the number of A wins (optionally accounting for ties), or a permutation test.
questions.choice_D: Pearson correlation between A and B outputs.
